sections.heading: Amendments, significant provisions & the Basic Structure

blocks.text: The Constitution is amended under **Article 368** by a **special majority** (and, for federal provisions, state ratification). The **Basic Structure doctrine (Kesavananda Bharati, 1973)** limits this power — Parliament cannot alter the Constitution's core identity.

rows: Three types — by **simple majority, special majority, special majority + ratification by half the states**.
**Kesavananda Bharati (1973)** — Parliament can amend but not destroy the **basic structure**.
Supremacy of Constitution, rule of law, judicial review, federalism, secularism, separation of powers, free elections.

items: Article 368; Basic Structure = Kesavananda Bharati (1973); Parliament can't destroy core.

prelimsPointers: Amendment procedure — **Article 368**; three types of majority.
**Basic Structure doctrine** — **Kesavananda Bharati case (1973)**.
Basic structure includes — **judicial review, federalism, secularism, rule of law, free & fair elections, separation of powers**.
**42nd Amendment (1976)** — the 'Mini-Constitution' (added FDs, Preamble words).
**44th Amendment (1978)** — removed Right to Property as FR; restored some post-Emergency safeguards.
**73rd & 74th Amendments (1992)** — Panchayati Raj & Urban Local Bodies.
**101st Amendment (2017)** — introduced **GST**.
mainsAngles: Explain the Basic Structure doctrine and its significance.

glossary.definition: The provision governing amendment of the Constitution.
The rule (Kesavananda Bharati, 1973) that Parliament cannot amend the Constitution's core identity.
A majority of the total membership plus two-thirds of members present and voting, needed for most amendments.

blocks.text: India's **federal division of powers** is set out in the **Seventh Schedule**, distributing subjects across the **Union, State and Concurrent Lists**, with **residuary powers to the Union** — a scheme tilted towards a **strong centre**.

rows: ~**97+ subjects** — defence, foreign affairs, banking, currency, railways; Parliament legislates.
~**66+ subjects** — police, public health, agriculture, land; State legislatures.
~**47+ subjects** — education, forests, marriage, criminal law; both legislate (**Union prevails** on conflict).

items: 7th Schedule = 3 lists; residuary with Union; on Concurrent conflict Union law prevails.
Education & forests moved to Concurrent by 42nd Amendment.

prelimsPointers: Division of powers — **Seventh Schedule**; **Union, State & Concurrent Lists**.
**Union List** (~97) — defence, foreign affairs, railways, currency.
**State List** (~66) — police, public order, public health, agriculture.
**Concurrent List** (~47) — education, forests, criminal law; **Union law prevails** on conflict (Art. 254).
**Residuary powers** vest in the **Union** (Article 248).
**Education & Forests** shifted from State to Concurrent by the **42nd Amendment**.
The scheme creates a **strong centre** ('federal with unitary bias').
mainsAngles: Analyse the division of legislative powers between the Union and the States.

glossary.definition: The schedule distributing subjects into the Union, State and Concurrent Lists.
Subjects on which both Parliament and states can legislate, with Union law prevailing on conflict.
Powers over subjects not in any list, vested in the Union (Art. 248).

blocks.text: The **Parliament** (Union legislature) is **bicameral** — the **Lok Sabha (House of the People) and Rajya Sabha (Council of States)** with the **President** — and **State Legislatures** may be uni- or bicameral. They **make laws, control the executive, and hold the purse**.

rows: Max **552**; directly elected; **5-yr** term; **Speaker**; controls **money bills**; no-confidence motion.
Max **250**; indirectly elected (state assemblies) + 12 nominated; **permanent (1/3 retire every 2 yrs)**; **Vice-President** chairs.
**Vidhan Sabha (Assembly)** always; **Vidhan Parishad (Council)** in some states (e.g. AP).
Legislation, budget, executive accountability, deliberation, representation.
**Money bills** originate only in Lok Sabha (Art. 110).

items: Lok Sabha (max 552, direct, money bills); Rajya Sabha (max 250, permanent, VP chairs).
AP has a Vidhan Parishad (Legislative Council).

prelimsPointers: Parliament = **President + Lok Sabha + Rajya Sabha** (bicameral).
**Lok Sabha** — max **552**; directly elected; term **5 years**; presided by the **Speaker**.
**Rajya Sabha** — max **250** (238 elected + 12 nominated); **permanent house** (1/3 retire every 2 yrs); chaired by the **Vice-President**.
**Money Bills** can be introduced only in the **Lok Sabha** (Article 110), on the President's recommendation.
**Rajya Sabha** has special powers — **Art. 249** (legislate on State List) & **Art. 312** (new AIS).
State legislature — **Vidhan Sabha** (all states) & **Vidhan Parishad** (some, incl. **Andhra Pradesh**).
A **no-confidence motion** can be moved only in the **Lok Sabha**.
mainsAngles: Compare the powers of the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha.

glossary.definition: The directly-elected lower house of Parliament, with primacy over money bills.
The indirectly-elected permanent upper house representing the states.
A bill on taxation/expenditure that can originate only in the Lok Sabha (Art. 110).

blocks.text: Legislatures enjoy **parliamentary privileges** (freedom of speech within the House, immunity from court proceedings) and conduct business through **motions, questions, sessions and committees** — the machinery of debate and executive accountability.

rows: **Freedom of speech in Parliament (Art. 105); immunity from court** for anything said/voted; regulate own procedure.
**Question Hour** (first hour) holds govt accountable; **Zero Hour** — Indian innovation.
**No-confidence, adjournment, calling attention, censure, cut motions**.
**PAC, Estimates, Public Undertakings**; Departmental Standing Committees; 'mini-parliaments'.

items: Privileges (Art 105); Zero Hour = Indian innovation; PAC/Estimates/PUC = financial committees.

prelimsPointers: **Parliamentary privileges** — **freedom of speech in the House (Art. 105)**; immunity from court for words/votes.
**Question Hour** — first hour; **Starred (oral), Unstarred (written), Short-notice** questions.
**Zero Hour** — an **Indian innovation** (raised without notice, after Question Hour).
**Adjournment motion** raises urgent public matters (Lok Sabha only); **No-confidence** tests majority.
Three sessions — **Budget, Monsoon, Winter**; **quorum = one-tenth** of total members.
Financial committees — **Public Accounts (PAC), Estimates, Public Undertakings**; PAC chaired by **Opposition**.
**Cut motions** are used to oppose demands for grants.
mainsAngles: Discuss parliamentary privileges and the role of committees in the legislature.

glossary.definition: Special rights of Houses/members ensuring free functioning, incl. immunity for speech within the House.
An Indian parliamentary innovation allowing members to raise matters without prior notice.
A financial committee (chaired by the Opposition) that audits government spending.

blocks.text: India is a **federation with a strong unitary bias** — described as **'quasi-federal'** (Wheare) or 'cooperative federalism'. Its working faces recurring **Centre-State tensions** over finances, governors, all-India services and autonomy.

rows: Dual polity, written/rigid constitution, division of powers, independent judiciary, bicameralism.
**Strong centre, single citizenship, All-India Services, Governor, emergency provisions, integrated judiciary, residuary powers with Union**.
**National (352), President's Rule (356), Financial (360)** — can make India unitary.
**Article 356 misuse, Governor's role, fiscal centralisation, river disputes, regionalism**.
**GST Council, NITI Aayog, Inter-State Council, Finance Commission**.

items: 'Quasi-federal' (Wheare); unitary features (strong centre, Governor, emergency, AIS).
Key tensions: Art 356, Governor's role, fiscal devolution; cooperative bodies = GST Council, ISC.

prelimsPointers: India is a **federation with a unitary bias** — 'quasi-federal' (K.C. Wheare).
The word 'federation' is **not used**; Art. 1 calls India a **'Union of States'**.
Unitary features — **strong centre, single citizenship, All-India Services, Governor, integrated judiciary, emergency provisions**.
**Article 356 (President's Rule)** — historically the most misused; curbed by **S.R. Bommai (1994)**.
**Governor's** role (discretion, reserving bills) is a recurring Centre-State flashpoint.
Cooperative-federalism bodies — **GST Council, Inter-State Council (Art. 263), Finance Commission, NITI Aayog**.
**Sarkaria & Punchhi Commissions** examined Centre-State relations.
mainsAngles: Examine the issues and challenges in Indian federalism.

glossary.definition: K.C. Wheare's description of India as federal in form but unitary in spirit.
The provision for President's Rule in a state, curbed by the S.R. Bommai judgment.
Centre and states working together through bodies like the GST Council and Inter-State Council.
